items.title: 11.4 The equivalence between mass and energy

source_refs.note: Topic 11.4 (PDF 256, printed 253). The catalogue keeps the printed heading 'Equilance'.

blocks.text: According to the special theory of relativity, mass and energy are distinct entities but are interconvertible. The total energy E and mass m of an object are related by E = mc^2 ... (11.4), where m depends on the speed of the object.

At rest, the energy equivalent of an object's mass m0 is called its rest mass energy E0: E0 = m0 c^2. As mc^2 is greater than m0 c^2, the difference of energy (mc^2 - m0 c^2) is due to the motion and represents the kinetic energy of the mass: K.E. = (m - m0) c^2.

From Eq. 11.4, the change in mass delta m due to a change in energy delta E is delta m = delta E/c^2. Because c^2 is a very large quantity, small changes in mass require very large changes in energy. In our everyday world energy changes are too small to produce measurable mass changes; however, the energy and mass changes in nuclear reactions are found to agree exactly with these equations.

blocks.title: Mass-energy relations
blocks.text: E = mc^2 (11.4); rest mass energy E0 = m0 c^2; kinetic energy K.E. = (m - m0) c^2; delta m = delta E/c^2.

blocks.prompt: The rest mass of an electron is 9.11 x 10^-31 kg; find its rest mass energy (numerical 11.4). An electron moves at 0.85c; find its total energy and kinetic energy in electron volts (numerical 11.5). If the rest mass m0 increases to m at high speed, what is the kinetic energy (MCQ 11.3)?

Describe Einstein's mass-energy equation. Why can we not observe its effects in everyday life (comprehensive question 11.2)? According to E = mc^2, is it possible to create a single electron from energy (constructed response 11.5)?
blocks.explanation: E = mc^2 says mass and energy are interconvertible, the conversion factor c^2 = 9 x 10^16 J kg^-1 being enormous; everyday energy changes, such as heating water, alter mass by amounts far too small to measure, while in nuclear reactions the mass lost appears as large amounts of energy. Not a single electron on its own: energy alone carries no electric charge, and charge must be conserved, so energy (for example a gamma-ray photon of at least 1.02 MeV) can create an electron only together with its antiparticle, a positron (pair production).

items: Mass and energy are interconvertible: E = mc^2 (11.4); E0 = m0 c^2; K.E. = (m - m0) c^2; delta m = delta E/c^2. Because c^2 is huge, everyday mass changes are unmeasurable, but nuclear reactions obey these equations exactly.
